outlooks.summary: Scattered severe storms are expected this afternoon through evening across much of the Dakotas into northwest Minnesota.

sections.title: Synopsis
sections.text: A shortwave trough will pivot northeastward from the northern Rockies into south central Canada, with minor height falls across the Dakotas by late in the day. At the surface, a low pressure trough will deepen over the western Dakota during the day, and will shift slowly eastward toward the MN border by Friday morning. A plume of mid to upper 60s F dewpoints is forecast to spread northwestward across the Dakotas, and will aid in destabilization. By evening, a broad southerly low-level jet will develop across the Plains, with strong theta-e advection across the Dakotas and MN. A warm front will also lift north toward the upper MS Valley overnight, also aiding storm development.

sections.title: Northern Plains
sections.text: Given shortwave ridging preceding the upper trough, much of the area will remain capped for most of the day. The exception will be across western SD, where hot temperatures and higher terrain will reduce CIN despite warm 700 mb temperatures. Storms are expected to form over western SD during the afternoon, and will be high-based. Various CAMs show an eventual cluster developing with strong outflow that will continue northeast across northern SD and southern ND. Although forecast soundings show CIN will be present, this scenario seems plausible should a strong cold pool develop. Sporadic hail will be possible as well. To the north, gradual cooling aloft should lead to a narrow zone of uncapped air near the front into northwest ND, with lift spreading eastward during the evening. While most of the severe storms will be north of the Canadian border, a few supercells are expected over northern ND, with significant hail possible as well as damaging winds. Steep lapse rates will lead to robust updrafts, with hodographs quite favorable for rotating storms. A tornado cannot be ruled out as well. ..Jewell/Bentley.. 06/14/2018

outlooks.summary: Scattered severe storms are expected this afternoon through tonight across much of the Dakotas into northwestern Minnesota.

sections.title: Northern Plains this afternoon through tonight
sections.text: A midlevel shortwave trough over the northern Rockies now will eject northeastward to southern Saskatchewan by early tonight. An associated lee cyclone now in southeastern MT will develop toward western SD, as a surface cold front progresses eastward into the western Dakotas this evening and the central Dakotas overnight. A surface warm front will move slowly northward across NE/SD today, allowing boundary-layer dewpoints of 65-70 F to spread northward from NE to the SD/ND border by late afternoon. Surface moisture will also increase across ND through advection and moisture mixing down from above the surface this morning. This moistening will occur beneath steep midlevel lapse rates, which in combination with daytime surface heating, will result in large buoyancy (MLCAPE in excess of 3000 J/kg) by this afternoon/evening across the Dakotas. The warm elevated mixed layer observed yesterday evening at RIW and this morning at UNR will also act to cap the boundary layer through much of the afternoon across the northern Plains. sections.title: Northeast MN into WI late tonight
sections.text: Some form of the Dakotas convection late today could survive as far east as northeastern MN after about 06z, though confidence in this scenario is low. A separate zone of elevated convection appears more probable in association with strengthening low-level warm advection, on the northeast edge of the feed of steep lapse rates and moisture from the warm sector. The strongest storms could produce isolated large hail overnight.

sections.title: IA today
sections.text: A swath of elevated storms are ongoing from northwestern into central IA in association with warm/moist advection in the 850-700 mb layer. These storms are occurring along the eastern edge of the steeper lapse rates, and have produced isolated large hail overnight. The threat for additional hail appears to be slowly diminishing as storms reach maximum coverage (but past peak intensity). Further weakening of the storms is expected from late morning into early afternoon as warm advection weakens. ..Thompson/Broyles.. 06/14/2018

outlooks.summary: Scattered to numerous severe storms are expected during the late afternoon and evening across parts of the Dakotas into northwest Minnesota. A couple tornadic storms, very large hail, and intense wind gusts are possible.

outlooks.summary: Scattered to numerous severe storms are expected during the late afternoon and evening across parts of the Dakotas into northwest Minnesota. A couple tornadic storms, very large hail, and intense wind gusts are possible. An isolated severe storm risk is possible across eastern Missouri and portions of west-central to southwest Illinois this afternoon.

sections.title: Eastern MO/west-central and southwest IL
sections.text: A Marginal severe risk has been introduced with this outlook issuance for part of the middle Mississippi Valley region with the greatest threats being for isolated damaging winds and hail. The potential for isolated strong to damaging wind gusts will progress to the south/southeast with the ongoing long-lived MCS, with the leading extent having recently moved into northeast MO and west-central IL per satellite/radar imagery and lightning data. The associated convective outflow boundary extended from the leading band of storms in west-central IL counties westward through northern MO, while a confluence boundary extended from the MO Bootheel into central MO. Observational data showed storms had also formed in south-central MO in vicinity of this latter boundary, where the environment has become very unstable with mixed-layer CAPE around 3000 J/kg. Although effective bulk shear is quite weak near this confluence boundary, pulse-type storms could pose an isolated severe risk. outlooks.summary: Severe storms with very large hail, damaging wind and a tornado or two are possible mainly across northern North Dakota near the Canadian border this evening. Scattered severe hail and wind is also expected across much of northern South Dakota and into North Dakota.

sections.title: Dakotas into northwest Minnesota
sections.text: Severe storms continue to track eastward along the international border, with very large hail, damaging wind and perhaps tornado potential. Local radars do show an outflow boundary extending southwestward and merging with the cold front into northwest ND, and some of the southernmost storms appear to be getting undercut. However, it is possible that some of the supercells may propagate in such a way as to keep the inflow surface based. Meanwhile, a separate cluster of strong to severe storms developed in very hot temperatures over western SD this afternoon, and is developing northeastward into south-central ND. Hail and wind remain possible with this activity, which may continue to spread northeastward this evening. The 00Z soundings from BIS and ABR show substantial capping and convective inhibition, but also strong instability. This should suppress any isolated, surface based development, with most of the activity associated with the ongoing cluster and outflows to the southwest. For more information see mesoscale discussions 736 and 737. ..Jewell.. 06/15/2018

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Ongoing MCS is moving southeast along a surface front with strong wind gusts and hail possible. This area will be upgraded into Marginal area with the 20z outlook.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: The MCS that continued overnight across Iowa has begun to accelerate to the southeast along a surface front and is moving at approximately 30-40 knots. A cold pool trailing the initial line of storms appears to be strengthening. The western portion of the line is moving into an area with higher moisture content (surface dewpoints in the low 70s) and the overall line of storms is moving along the buoyancy gradient. Severe hail and strong wind gusts at 35-45 knots have been observed in the last 30 minutes as the line of storms have intensified. Strong wind gusts and marginal severe hail are possible as this line of storms moves southeast over the next couple of hours. HRRR and HRRR-P do not resolve this complex well leading to some uncertainty on how long/far these line of storms will persist into the afternoon/evening. However, pulse storms forming across eastern Missouri may merge into the trailing outflow and could result in a marginal severe threat persisting into the afternoon.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: A few supercells are expected to develop later this afternoon/evening across western and northern North Dakota. Tornadoes, very large hail, and damaging wind gusts are possible.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: A mid-level shortwave trough is currently moving across southern British Columbia/Alberta generating some mid-level clouds and elevated convection across Montana. A surface low is located in eastern Montana near Glendive, a remnant outflow boundary is oriented east-west across northeastern Montana and into northwestern North Dakota, and a weak warm front is analyzed across northern North Dakota. These features should help focus forcing for ascent across portions of far western/northern North Dakota in the next few hours. Surface heating and the outflow boundary/weak warm front should destabilize the low-mid levels and break a robust cap located at 800-700 mb, as sampled by the 19z BIS sounding. Increasing low-level moisture (surface dewpoints mid to upper 60s and mean mixing ratios of 11-14 g/kg), strong low-level shear/hodograph curvature (effective bulk shear of 50-60 knots and effective SRH upwards of 200 m2/s2), and strong buoyancy (forecast MLCAPE in excess of 2500 J/kg) will support development of a few supercells in western/northern North Dakota, most likely along/near the US/Canada border. The main threats for these storms will be very large hail, damaging wind gusts, and tornadoes. A strong tornado appears possible near the US/Canada border in northern North Dakota around 23-03z. These storms should remain discrete for several hours before merging downstream to form a late evening/overnight MCS.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Thunderstorm development is forecast generally after 21Z over far western portions of SD. Once thunderstorms develop and intensify, large hail and severe gusts (60-70 mph) are possible with the stronger thunderstorms. An evolution of a thunderstorm cluster growing upscale into a severe-wind producing MCS will seemingly occur this evening and significant severe gusts (greater than 75 mph) are possible during the mature phase of the MCS.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Visible-satellite imagery shows a high-based cumulus field beginning to develop east of the Black Hills with a mid-level accas shield moving into western SD from northeastern WY. Surface observations show temperatures have warmed to around 100 degrees F near Rapid City with dewpoints in the low-mid 50s. Farther northeast, richer moisture characterized by upper 60s to near 70 dewpoints will likely be maintained as a strong capping inversion aids in increasing moisture quality as deeper boundary-layer mixing occurs. Much of the large-scale forcing for ascent is forecast to pass to the north near the ND/Canadian border. Yet, very deep boundary layer circulations and convective temperatures likely being breached will help facilitate convective initiation over western SD and northwest NE from eastern WY. As the mid-level convection over northeast WY moves downstream into an environment with richer low-level moisture (located near the cumulus field), high/surface-based thunderstorm development is expected near and after 21Z. The 19Z Rapid City RAOB showed a nearly dry adiabatic surface-500 mb lapse rate and southwesterly flow gradually strengthening with height and yielding around 35 kt effective shear. The moderate to strong buoyancy farther east/northeast coupled with deep-layer shear favorable for organized storms, will favor severe thunderstorm development. Large hail and isolated severe gusts are the primary threats over western SD before becoming predominately a wind threat (perhaps significant) into central portions of SD and south-central ND.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Isolated large hail and damaging winds are possible this evening.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Initial line of storms dropping south in eastern Missouri have become increasingly outflow dominant through time as they move further away from the stronger mid-level flow. These storms are moving into an airmass which has previously been overturned and has ongoing convection which will limit the severe threat in western Illinois and far eastern Missouri into the evening. The western edge of the outflow boundary will have the best opportunity for strong to severe storms into the evening as new storms form along boundary interactions where MUCAPE exceeds 3000 J/kg. 0-6 km shear around 25 knots via LSX VWP suggests limits to updraft longevity will preclude a more organized severe threat, but the instability will support isolated large hail and damaging winds as updraft cores collapse.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Large hail threat will continue with convection over northeast North Dakotas. Limited areal coverage will preclude a severe thunderstorm watch over the next few hours.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Southern extent of long-lived convection has progressed across northern ND and has exited Tornado Watch 177. This activity is likely elevated in nature with warm advection the primary forcing mechanism. MRMS hail algorithm continues to exhibit large hail with a storm over Towner County. Current speed/movement suggests this activity should propagate into Cavalier County and perhaps Pembina County with time. With warm advection expected to focus along the Canadian side of the international border there is insufficient area to issue a watch at this time per collaboration with Grand Forks WFO.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Large hail and strong winds should accompany convection this evening.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Convection is gradually increasing across western SD into extreme southwest ND. This activity is initiating along eastern edge of very steep lapse rate plume where surface temperature earlier warmed in excess of 100F. Initial convection appears to be high based but there is some concern updrafts may begin to draw more buoyant low-level parcels as updrafts encounter higher theta-e environment. MRMS hail algorithm depicts large hail with updrafts over northwestern SD and hail can be expected with other robust convection this evening. Additionally, gusty winds may be noted with this high-based convection as temp/dew point spreads are considerable across western SD. ..Darrow.. 06/14/2018 ...Please see www.spc.noaa.gov for graphic product...

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Tornado threat continues across northwest ND...especially near the international border.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Strong low-level warm advection appears to be the primary forcing mechanism for deep convection along/just north of the international border. Several longer-lived supercells have progressed into southeast SK/southwest MB and this activity is expected to focus along the border region into the late evening hours. South of the warm front, higher-based convection has struggled to develop across western ND. Several attempts at sustained updrafts have failed and it's not entirely clear how convection will evolve over the next few hours; although, storms should eventually focus along the cold front as it surges into this part of the watch. Greatest tornado threat should focus along the Canadian border. ..Darrow.. 06/14/2018 ...Please see www.spc.noaa.gov for graphic product...

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Tornado threat is expected to increase across northeast North Dakota as supercells spread into the upper Red River Valley.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Low-level warm advection is expected to focus across the upper Red River Valley region late this evening as LLJ strengthens over the eastern Dakotas into western MN. Several long-lived supercells continue along the international border region which should propagate east of WW177 in the next 1-2 hours. Severe threat will increase across northeastern ND as this activity advances east. Tornado watch appears warranted downstream to account for this scenario.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: A cluster of strong to severe storms is expected to persist for a few more hours with isolated large hail and damaging winds possible.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: The cluster of storms which has been persistent along the Mississippi River all day is moving into a more favorable thermodynamic airmass. This has led to additional storm development in Bollinger County, Missouri. Given these storms are moving towards an area with mid to upper 70s dewpoints and MUCAPE of 3000 to 4000 J/kg, additional strong storms may develop in the next hour or two. The primary threat will be isolated large hail and damaging winds beneath the heaviest cores before they quickly dissipate due to weak effective shear. While diurnal cooling should bring this activity to an end, a very moist boundary layer will lead to slow cooling and may allow activity to persist a bit longer into the overnight hours than might otherwise be expected in a low shear, surface-based instability environment.

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Severe threat is expected to gradually sag southeast across ww179. Hail is becoming the primary risk, although wind may be noted as well.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Corridor of low-level warm advection remains focused across the upper Red River Valley. This appears mostly responsible for the maintenance of ongoing convection across northeastern ND. Over the last few hours earlier supercell structures have morphed into clusters and short line segments. This evolution appears more favorable for hail, and perhaps some wind, as southwest-northeast oriented complex shifts into northwest MN. ..Darrow.. 06/15/2018 ...Please see www.spc.noaa.gov for graphic product...

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Thunderstorm activity is expected to continue a general weakening trends as it spreads across much of northwestern and north central Minnesota through 3-5 AM CDT. A new severe weather watch is not anticipated.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: Considerable weakening of the thunderstorm cluster now near/northwest through northeast of Grafton ND, into the Roseau MN vicinity, appears well underway. Scattered strong cells do linger to the southwest of Fargo, with this activity still likely supported by inflow of seasonably moist boundary layer air. In general, convection appears largely driven by ascent associated with a fairly broad area of strong low-level warm advection, which extends eastward across much of Minnesota. However, this is largely beneath the nose of a broad plume of very warm elevated mixed layer air, which probably is beginning to suppress convective development. Weakening trends probably will continue into the 08-10Z time frame. As 30-40 kt southwesterly deep layer mean flow advects convection into and through much of northwestern/north central Minnesota, activity will become increasingly displaced from inflow emanating from a moist low-level environment over the Missouri Valley, above cooler and more stable surface based air associated with a surface high centered over the Great Lakes. ..Kerr.. 06/15/2018 ...Please see www.spc.noaa.gov for graphic product...

mesoscale_discussions.summary: Increasing thunderstorm development is expected through the 4-6 AM CDT time frame, with the risk for large hail the primary potential severe hazard. Due to the generally isolated nature of the expected threat, a severe weather watch is not anticipated, but trends will be monitored.
mesoscale_discussions.discussion: The 40-50 kt low-level jet continues to gradually veer to an increasingly southwesterly component while shifting east of the Dakotas into the upper Mississippi Valley. Downstream of a short wave trough now progressing northeastward into southern Saskatchewan, a zone of enhanced low-level warm advection is forecast to develop across the Minnesota Arrowhead and western Lake Superior vicinity into north central Wisconsin. This is generally just east of the nose of the warm and more strongly capping elevated mixed layer plume emanating from the Great Basin. Models suggest that this will coincide with elevated moisture return (within the 850-700 mb layer) underrunning the cap, which may contribute to rapid destabilization and increasing thunderstorm development through the 09-11Z time frame. This will generally be based above a relatively cool/stable surface based air mass associated with a surface high centered over the Great Lakes. However, the development of moderately large CAPE, in the presence of at least modest vertical shear within the convective layer, probably will be sufficient to support at least some risk for severe hail.
